# Issuers, integrations and curators

Source: https://lowob.com/research/issuers-integrations-and-curators/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-22 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: When paid channels are closed, distribution in crypto comes from the people who already have a reason to want you to succeed: issuers, integrations, curators and ecosystems. The closure is specific: Google bans ads for DeFi trading protocols, token liquidity pools and initial coin offerings in every market, and the UK bans refer-a-friend bonuses for crypto promotions. Work the list of people who gain when you grow before you spend a dollar on reach, and keep every piece of copy free of APYs and yield promises.

## Key points

- Sort every proposed channel into open, restricted or closed bands, per market, before setting any budget.
- Some closures are global: Google prohibits ads for DeFi trading protocols, liquidity pools, crypto loans and ICOs regardless of location.
- Every issuer whose asset you support is a free BD list; most will promote a new use for their asset if asked with something specific.
- Curators set the caps and risk limits for vault capital; pitch them inventory and risk parameters, not TVL.
- No APYs, no yield promises and no screenshots of thin dashboards in any copy, including KOL copy.

## The three bands for crypto

[Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/) laid out distribution when platforms are closed. Crypto needs its own version because the closure is tighter and the exceptions change often.

| Band | What sits in it (policies checked 16 November 2026) | How to treat it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open | Owned media, integrations, partner co-marketing, ecosystem programmes, answer engines | Build here first; this is most of your distribution |
| Restricted | Google ads for exchanges and software wallets, with certification and local registration such as FCA registration in the UK or MiCA authorisation in the EU; TikTok crypto ads in markets that permit them, through a sales representative; paid placements and sponsorships with disclosure and legal review | Use sparingly, with every piece of copy reviewed before it runs |
| Closed | Google ads for DeFi trading protocols, token liquidity pools, crypto loans, unregulated dApps and ICOs, in every market; crypto ads in markets where TikTok lists them as not allowed; anything that promises returns | Do not plan around it; policy can shift, but not on your timeline |

Put every channel you are considering into a band before you budget for it. Most teams discover that their plan was mostly in the closed band and their time was mostly in the restricted one.

The restricted band does move. Google opened exchange and wallet advertising in Canada in July 2025, Argentina in September 2025 and Indonesia in February 2026, each subject to local registration and Google certification. For a DeFi protocol, none of those changes applied. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers how the sorting works across platforms.

## The free BD list

Here is the list you already have. Every asset you support, list, lend against or route through has an issuer. That issuer wants more venues, more liquidity and more use for their asset.

You are a new place for their asset to be used. That is a reason to promote you, and most will if asked.

Work the list properly. Name a contact at each issuer. Offer something specific: a launch announcement, a joint piece of content, a shared integration guide, a slot in their community call. Ask for the same in return, in writing, with dates.

| Issuer BD list field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Asset and issuer | The token, and the team behind it |
| Named contact | One person, not a general channel |
| What you offer | Launch announcement, joint content, integration guide or community call slot |
| What you ask | The same, in their channels |
| Dates | Agreed in writing |
| Result | What it produced, recorded after launch |

This is BD, not marketing. It takes one person with a spreadsheet and a calendar. It is the cheapest distribution you will ever buy, and almost nobody does it systematically. The wider pattern, using partners' customer overlap to win and keep users, is covered in [what is ecosystem-led growth?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ecosystem-led-growth/)

## Integrations: go where the users already are

A user in crypto rarely goes to a new site to find a new product. They find it inside the tools they already use.

That means wallets, front-ends, aggregators and lending markets are distribution, not just engineering. Each integration puts you in front of an active user at the moment they are deciding what to do with capital.

Treat the integration roadmap as a channel plan. Rank by where your target users already spend time, not by which team replied to your email first. Ship the integration, then do the co-marketing that goes with it. An integration nobody announces is a channel nobody uses. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to agree roles and obligations with each integration partner before launch.

> An integration nobody announces is a channel nobody uses.

## Curators and allocators: sell the inventory, not the TVL

In DeFi there is a layer of people whose job is to decide where capital goes. Curators, vault managers, allocators, risk teams at treasuries. They are a distribution channel, and most teams pitch them wrong.

The role is formal on some protocols. Morpho's documentation describes a curator as the party that sets a vault's risk parameters and liquidity rules, decides which adapters can route vault capital, and defines exposure limits, or caps, on risk factors such as collateral, oracle and protocol exposure. Curators appoint allocators, who make day-to-day allocation decisions within those limits, and most significant curator actions sit behind a timelock so depositors can exit.

The wrong pitch is a TVL number and a growth chart. They have seen it, and they know how it was built.

The right pitch is inventory. What can they deploy into, at what size, with what risk parameters, and what happens when they need to exit. Give them the documentation a risk committee would ask for, before they ask.

| Allocator pack section | What it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | What capital can be deployed into, and in which markets |
| Size | Depth at which the position still behaves as described |
| Risk parameters | Collateral, oracle and protocol exposure, and the caps that apply |
| Exit path | How and how fast capital comes out under stress |
| Documentation | Audits, governance powers, timelocks and incident history |

One serious allocator who understands the position is worth more than a thousand wallets that arrived for a point multiplier. Build the materials for that allocator and the rest follows.

## Foundations, grants and KOLs

Ecosystem foundations fund teams because they want activity on their chain. That makes them a distribution partner, not only a funding source. [Part 17](https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/) made the point that chain choice is a distribution decision. Here is where you collect on it.

Ask every grant for what comes with it: announcement slots, event placement, introductions to the wallets and front-ends in their ecosystem, co-marketing from their own channels. If a grant offers money with no distribution, weigh it against one that offers both.

KOLs are a legitimate channel when done in the open. Paid partnership disclosed as such, every time. The US Federal Trade Commission's guidance says the disclosure belongs in the endorsement itself, in plain words such as "ad" or "sponsored", and in the video for video content. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority's 2024 guidance says influencers who promote a regulated product without approval from an authorised firm may be committing a criminal offence. The claims rules below apply to their copy as much as to yours. A KOL who will not disclose is a liability with a follower count.

## Claims rules and answer engines

Every piece of copy, from a landing page to a reply in a community channel, follows the claims register from [Part 2](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/). In crypto, that register has two hard lines.

No APYs. No yield promises. Not projected, not historical, not "up to". If a number about returns appears in your copy, it appears with context, a date and a reviewer's sign-off, or it does not appear. That is **lowob**'s rule and it is stricter than most regulation, which is the point.

The regulation is moving the same way. The FCA's cryptoasset promotions regime, in force since 8 October 2023, requires promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading, carry specific risk warnings, include a 24-hour cooling-off period for first-time investors, and bans refer-a-friend bonuses. Under the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, Article 7 requires marketing communications to be clearly identifiable, fair, clear and not misleading, and consistent with the crypto-asset white paper, and none may be disseminated before the white paper is published.

Never screenshot a thin dashboard. A chart with three days of data and one large depositor is not proof of traction. It is evidence you were in a hurry. Wait until the picture is real.

Answer engines now shape a large share of how people first hear about a product. They read your documentation, your integration guides and your public records, and they repeat what is there. Write those pages plainly, keep them current, and make sure the claims in them are the ones you are willing to defend. Our piece on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) covers the mechanics.

## lowob takeaways

- **Band every channel per market first.** Some crypto closures, such as Google's ban on DeFi protocol ads, are global.
- **Work the issuer list systematically.** A named contact, a specific offer and dates in writing.
- **Rank integrations by where users already are, and announce each one.** Unannounced integrations carry no one.
- **Pitch curators inventory and risk parameters.** Caps, exposures and exit paths, not TVL.
- **Hold the claims line everywhere.** No APYs, no yield promises, no thin dashboards, disclosed KOLs.

## Common questions

### How do crypto projects market when ad platforms are closed to them?

Build mostly in open channels: owned media, issuer co-marketing, integrations, ecosystem programmes and answer engines. Use restricted paid placements sparingly with review, and do not plan around closed channels such as Google ads for DeFi protocols.

### Can DeFi protocols advertise on Google?

No. Google's cryptocurrency policy prohibits ads for DeFi trading protocols, token liquidity pools, crypto loans and initial coin offerings regardless of location. Exchanges and software wallets can advertise in approved markets once certified.

### How should I pitch a DeFi protocol to curators and allocators?

Pitch inventory, not TVL: what they can deploy into, at what size, with what risk parameters, and what happens when they exit, with the documentation a risk committee would ask for.

### Can crypto projects use KOLs for marketing?

Yes, when done in the open: paid partnerships disclosed in the content every time, with the same claims rules applied to their copy as to yours, and with local promotion rules such as the UK's checked first.
